title: Metallic Taste After Drinking: Causes, Fixes, and When to Worry
excerpt: Why your mouth tastes like metal after drinking alcohol: dry mouth, reflux, gums, and medicines like metronidazole. How to get rid of it fast and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why your mouth tastes like metal after drinking: dry mouth, reflux, gums, and drugs like metronidazole. Fast fixes and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a metallic taste in your mouth the morning after drinking is usually harmless and fades within a day. The most common causes are a dry mouth (alcohol cuts saliva, and saliva is what normally washes stray tastes away), stomach acid creeping up your throat overnight, and a little blood from irritated gums. The one cause you should not shrug off is medication. If you are taking **metronidazole (Flagyl)** or a related antibiotic, a metallic taste is a known side effect of the drug itself, and drinking on it can cause a nasty reaction. A metallic taste that lasts for days, keeps coming back, or arrives with other symptoms also deserves a doctor's look.

**The quick fixes:** drink water steadily, rinse your mouth, brush and floss gently, chew sugar-free gum or suck a sugar-free lemon drop to get saliva flowing, and eat something bland. If you had reflux overnight, sit upright and skip coffee and greasy food for the morning. If you are on any prescription medicine, check its leaflet for "taste changes" and for alcohol warnings before you drink again.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most hangover metallic taste clears within 24 hours. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist if** the taste lasts longer than a few days, keeps returning even when you haven't been drinking, started after a new medicine, or comes with mouth sores, swollen or bleeding gums, or a loss of taste or smell. **Get urgent care (call 911 in the US) if** you are vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, have black or tarry stools, have chest pain, or notice yellow skin or eyes, confusion, or severe stomach pain. **If you drank while taking metronidazole or tinidazole** and now have flushing, a pounding heart, vomiting, or trouble breathing, get medical help right away. If you drink heavily most days and feel shaky, sweaty, or confused when you stop, that is a withdrawal sign, and a doctor can help you stop safely.

## Why Your Mouth Tastes Like Metal After Drinking

Doctors call a changed or unpleasant taste **dysgeusia**. A metallic version of it is one of the most common forms, and it has many possible triggers. Alcohol touches several of them at once, which is why it shows up so often after a night out.

Here are the main causes, roughly from most to least common.

### 1. Dry mouth (the most likely culprit)

Alcohol makes you pee more because it blocks a hormone (vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone) that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. You also tend to sleep with your mouth open after drinking, and you may snore. All of that leaves your mouth dry by morning.

Saliva does a lot more than keep your mouth wet. It dilutes and washes away taste molecules, keeps the balance of bacteria in check, and buffers acids. When there's less of it, leftover tastes linger, bacteria multiply, and your taste buds sit in a thicker, more concentrated film. Many people describe the result as stale, sour, or metallic.

This is the cause in most cases, and it's also the easiest to fix. Our guide to [dry mouth after drinking](/never-hungover/dry-mouth-after-drinking) goes deeper on why it happens and what works.

### 2. Acid reflux overnight

Alcohol relaxes the ring of muscle at the bottom of your esophagus (the lower esophageal sphincter) that normally keeps stomach contents where they belong. It also increases stomach acid and irritates the stomach lining. Add a late meal, lying flat, and a few hours of sleep, and acid can travel up toward your throat and mouth.

Reflux usually tastes sour or bitter, but plenty of people describe it as metallic, especially when it's mild and they only notice the aftertaste on waking. Clues that reflux is behind yours: a burning feeling behind your breastbone, a hoarse voice or sore throat in the morning, a cough, or a taste that gets worse when you bend over or lie down. If this sounds familiar, our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) covers what helps.

### 3. Vomiting

If you were sick, stomach acid and bile passed through your mouth. That alone can leave a bitter, sour, or metallic taste for hours. Vomiting also dries you out further and can irritate your throat. Rinse with plain water (or water with a pinch of baking soda) rather than brushing straight away, because acid softens tooth enamel for a short while and brushing right after can wear it down.

### 4. A small amount of blood from your gums

Blood tastes metallic because of the iron in it. Alcohol, especially when combined with a dry mouth and skipping your bedtime brushing, can leave gums puffy and irritated. Brushing too hard the next morning, or eating crunchy bar snacks, can make them bleed a little. You may not see the blood, but you'll taste it.

If you notice pink on your toothbrush or in the sink regularly, that points to gum inflammation (gingivitis), which is worth raising with a dentist. Occasional light bleeding after a rough night isn't an emergency.

### 5. Congestion and sinus irritation

Most of what we call "taste" is actually smell. Alcohol widens blood vessels in your nose and can make it stuffy, and some people react to compounds in wine and beer (such as histamine or sulfites) with a blocked or runny nose. When your sense of smell is muffled, food and drink can taste flat or oddly metallic, and postnasal drip adds its own unpleasant taste.

### 6. Smoking or vaping while drinking

Lots of people who don't usually smoke will have a cigarette or a vape on a night out. Smoke and vapor dry the mouth further, coat the tongue, and leave their own bitter, metallic residue. If the taste is worst on nights you smoked, that's a strong hint.

## The Medication Question: Metronidazole and Other Drugs

This is the section that matters most, because here the metallic taste is a sign of something to take seriously.

### Metronidazole (Flagyl)

Metronidazole is an antibiotic used for bacterial vaginosis, some stomach and gut infections, dental infections, and trichomoniasis, among other things. A metallic taste is one of its best-known side effects, and it's listed on the drug's label. It happens whether or not you drink.

The bigger issue is alcohol. Metronidazole carries a warning against drinking during treatment and for at least three days afterward, because the combination has been reported to cause a **disulfiram-like reaction**. In plain words, that means your body may struggle to clear acetaldehyde, the toxic by-product of alcohol, leading to flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and a racing heart. How often this truly happens is debated in the medical literature, but the warning stands and it's the advice your prescriber and pharmacist will give you.

So if you have a metallic taste and you're on metronidazole, there are two separate things going on:

- **The taste itself** is probably the drug. It usually fades within a few days of finishing the course.
- **Any drinking** while on it, or within three days after, is a risk you should avoid.

If you've already had a drink on metronidazole, don't panic, but don't drink more. Our guides on [metronidazole and alcohol](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol) and [what to do if you accidentally drank on metronidazole](/never-hungover/accidentally-drank-on-metronidazole) explain the timing and the warning signs. If you feel very unwell, call a doctor or pharmacist, or Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** in the US.

**Tinidazole**, a close cousin of metronidazole, carries a similar alcohol warning and can also cause a metallic or bitter taste.

### Paxlovid

The COVID antiviral Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir with ritonavir) is well known for causing an unpleasant bitter or metallic taste, often nicknamed "Paxlovid mouth." Alcohol doesn't cause it, but if you're on Paxlovid and notice the taste, that's the likely source. Ritonavir also interacts with many other medicines, so it's worth checking with a pharmacist before drinking. See our guide to [Paxlovid and alcohol](/never-hungover/paxlovid-and-alcohol) for more.

### Other medicines that can change taste

Many drugs list taste changes as a side effect. Some well-known examples:

- **Certain antibiotics**, such as clarithromycin
- **Lithium**, used for bipolar disorder
- **Some blood pressure medicines**, notably ACE inhibitors such as captopril
- **Some antidepressants and anti-anxiety medicines**
- **Allopurinol**, used for gout
- **Prenatal vitamins and iron, zinc, or multivitamin supplements**
- **Cancer treatments**, including chemotherapy

If the metallic taste began around the same time you started a new medicine or supplement, the medicine is a more likely explanation than the drinking. Don't stop a prescribed medicine on your own. Mention the taste to your doctor or pharmacist, who can tell you whether it's expected and whether alcohol is safe with that drug. For a broader look, our [antibiotics and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol) covers which antibiotics have real alcohol warnings and which don't.

## Could It Be What You Drank?

Sometimes the metallic taste is coming from the drink itself, or from what you paired it with.

**Copper mugs.** Moscow mules are often served in copper mugs. Copper can leach into acidic drinks (lime juice and ginger beer are both acidic), and too much copper can cause a metallic taste, nausea, and stomach upset. US food safety guidance advises against letting copper touch acidic foods and drinks, which is why most food-safe copper mugs are lined with stainless steel or nickel. If your mug was unlined, that may explain the taste.

**Wine with seafood.** Researchers in Japan reported in 2009 (in the *Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry*) that iron in some wines helps create an unpleasant fishy, metallic aftertaste when the wine is paired with certain seafood. If the taste hit during dinner, the pairing could be part of it.

**Tannins and bitterness.** Red wine, strong black tea in cocktails, and some aged spirits are high in tannins, which feel drying and astringent. Ethanol itself also activates bitter taste receptors. These sensations sometimes get described as metallic, even though that's not quite what they are. Our article on [why alcohol tastes bad](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-taste-bad) explains how bitter and burn work.

**Canned drinks and hard seltzers.** Some people swear they taste "can" in canned drinks. Modern cans are lined, so the drink isn't usually touching bare metal, but a strong smell of the can rim while you drink can influence the taste. This is minor and harmless.

**Pine nuts.** It sounds odd, but some people develop a bitter, metallic taste lasting days to weeks after eating certain pine nuts, a reaction known as "pine mouth." If you had pesto or a salad with pine nuts on your night out, it's worth considering. It goes away on its own.

## When a Metallic Taste Isn't About Last Night

If you keep getting a metallic taste, even on days you didn't drink, it's probably not a hangover symptom. Other common causes include:

- **Colds, flu, sinus infections, and COVID**, which can all change taste and smell
- **Pregnancy**, especially early on, when a metallic taste is a commonly reported symptom
- **Dental problems**, such as gum disease, an infected tooth, or old metal fillings or crowns
- **Low zinc or vitamin B12**, both of which are linked to taste changes. Heavy drinking can lower zinc levels over time, which our guide to [zinc and alcohol](/never-hungover/zinc-and-alcohol) covers in more detail.
- **Kidney or liver problems**, which can change both taste and breath. These come with other symptoms (tiredness, swelling, itching, yellowing of the skin or eyes, changes in urine), not a metallic taste on its own.
- **Diabetes and blood sugar problems**, which can cause dry mouth and taste changes

None of these are reasons to worry over a single bad morning. They are reasons to see a doctor if the taste becomes a pattern.

## How to Get Rid of a Metallic Taste After Drinking

Most of these work by bringing saliva back, washing the taste off your tongue, or settling your stomach.

### Rehydrate steadily

Sip water through the morning rather than chugging a liter at once. A drink with some electrolytes (sodium and potassium) can help if you were sick or sweated a lot. If you wonder how much alcohol really dries you out, see our explainer on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).

### Clean your mouth gently

- Brush your teeth and tongue with a soft brush. A lot of the taste lives in the film on your tongue.
- Floss, especially if you skipped it last night.
- Rinse with water, or with a cup of water mixed with about half a teaspoon of baking soda, which neutralizes acid.
- Skip alcohol-based mouthwash for now. It can dry your mouth further. An alcohol-free rinse is fine.
- If you vomited, rinse first and wait about 30 minutes before brushing.

### Get saliva flowing

- Chew sugar-free gum, ideally one with xylitol.
- Suck on a sugar-free lemon drop or a slice of lemon or lime. Sour flavors are strong saliva triggers.
- Eat something crunchy and fresh, like an apple or cucumber.

### Use flavors that push back

Citrus, mint, ginger, and herbs like parsley can mask a metallic taste. Some people find that cold foods taste better than hot ones while their taste is off, and that plastic or wooden cutlery helps if metal forks taste unpleasant.

### Settle reflux

- Sit or stand upright for a while after eating.
- Skip coffee, orange juice, spicy food, and greasy food for the morning. They all tend to aggravate reflux.
- An over-the-counter antacid can help if you have heartburn as well. Our guide to the [best antacids after drinking](/never-hungover/best-antacid-after-drinking) compares the options.
- Tonight, finish eating two to three hours before bed and try raising the head of your bed slightly.

### Give it time

A hangover-related metallic taste usually fades within a day as your saliva, hydration, and stomach settle. If it hasn't improved after two or three days, revisit the causes above and consider seeing a doctor or dentist.

## How to Prevent It Next Time

You can't always prevent a metallic taste, but you can make it much less likely.

- **Drink water between drinks.** One glass of water per alcoholic drink is a simple, widely used rule of thumb.
- **Eat before and during drinking.** Food slows alcohol absorption and gives your stomach something besides alcohol to deal with.
- **Stop eating and drinking a couple of hours before bed** if you're prone to reflux.
- **Brush and floss before bed,** no matter how late it is. This one habit tackles the gum and bacteria causes.
- **Keep water by the bed** and sip if you wake up dry.
- **Skip the cigarette or vape.**
- **Check your medicines.** Before drinking on any prescription, read the leaflet for alcohol warnings or ask a pharmacist. With metronidazole and tinidazole, the answer is simply don't.
- **Pace yourself.** Fewer drinks spread over more time means less dehydration, less reflux, and less of everything else that causes a rough morning. Our guide to [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people take DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree, as part of their drinking-night routine. It has been studied mostly in animals and in lab settings for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver, with only limited human data. It's promising, not proven.

To be clear about this page's topic: there is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats a metallic taste. It won't fix dry mouth, reflux, or bleeding gums, and it does nothing for a taste caused by medication. It also does **not** make it safe to drink while on metronidazole or tinidazole.

If you're interested in DHM for general hangover support alongside the habits above, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [best DHM supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-dhm-supplements) compares brands, and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when. If you take prescription medication, check with your pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- A metallic taste after drinking is usually from dry mouth, overnight reflux, vomiting, or mildly irritated gums. It typically clears within a day.
- Water, gentle brushing, sugar-free gum, sour or minty flavors, and a bland breakfast are the fastest fixes.
- If you're on **metronidazole or tinidazole**, the drug is likely causing the taste, and you should not drink during treatment or for at least three days after.
- Other medicines, supplements, pregnancy, infections, and dental problems can cause the same taste, so a taste that lingers or keeps returning is worth a check-up.
- Get urgent care for vomiting blood, black stools, chest pain, yellow skin or eyes, or a severe reaction after drinking on an antibiotic.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my mouth taste like metal after drinking alcohol?**

The most common reason is dry mouth. Alcohol makes you lose fluid and you often sleep with your mouth open, so there's less saliva to wash tastes away by morning. Overnight acid reflux, vomiting, and a little blood from irritated gums are the other usual causes. Certain medicines, especially the antibiotic metronidazole, can also cause a metallic taste.

**How long does a metallic taste last after drinking?**

When it comes from dehydration or reflux after a night out, it usually fades within a day once you rehydrate, eat, and clean your mouth. If it lasts more than two or three days, keeps coming back on days you didn't drink, or started with a new medicine, talk to a doctor, pharmacist, or dentist.

**Is a metallic taste after drinking a sign of liver damage?**

Not usually. Liver disease can change taste and breath, but it comes with other symptoms such as ongoing tiredness, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, itching, swelling in the belly or legs, or easy bruising. A metallic taste on its own after one night of drinking is almost always from dry mouth or reflux. If you drink heavily on a regular basis and notice any of those other signs, see a doctor.

**Can you drink alcohol on metronidazole if you already have a metallic taste?**

No. The metallic taste is a common side effect of metronidazole itself, and drinking during treatment or for at least three days after the last dose is advised against because of the risk of a reaction that can cause flushing, vomiting, headache, and a racing heart. Follow your prescriber's instructions. If you already drank and feel very unwell, get medical help.

**What gets rid of a metallic taste in the mouth fast?**

Drink water, brush your teeth and tongue gently, and rinse with water or a little baking soda in water. Then get saliva flowing with sugar-free gum or a sugar-free lemon drop, and eat something fresh and bland. Citrus, mint, and ginger can help mask the taste while it fades.

**Why do Moscow mules sometimes taste metallic?**

Moscow mules are acidic, and when they're served in unlined copper mugs some copper can leach into the drink, which can cause a metallic taste and, in larger amounts, nausea. Food safety guidance in the US advises against letting copper touch acidic drinks, so look for mugs lined with stainless steel or nickel.

**Could a metallic taste after drinking be acid reflux?**

Yes. Alcohol relaxes the muscle that keeps stomach acid out of your esophagus and increases acid production, so reflux overnight is common after drinking. It often tastes sour or bitter but can come across as metallic. Signs that reflux is the cause include heartburn, a hoarse voice or sore throat in the morning, and a taste that gets worse when you lie down.

**Does DHM help with a metallic taste after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats a metallic taste. The taste usually comes from dry mouth, reflux, or medication, and DHM doesn't address those. Water, oral hygiene, and checking your medicines are what help.
